title: Voice- / gesture-controlled robot
desc: A Teachable Machine model drives an Arduino robot — an AI × Arduino crossover
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno R3
  • 1 x L298N Dual H-Bridge Motor Driver Module
  • 2 x DC Gear Motors with wheels
  • 1 x Caster/support wheel
  • 1 x Robot chassis plate (acrylic or plywood, two-layer or single-layer)
  • 1 x Battery pack — 4xAA holder with switch or 7.4V Li-ion pack
  • 1 x Jumper wire pack (Male-Male and Male-Female)
  • 1 x USB cable (Type A to Type B, for Uno)
  • 1 x Small breadboard (optional, for prototyping connections)
  • 1 x Laptop with Google Chrome browser and a working webcam and/or microphone (school/student-provided)
  • Screws, double-sided tape, or zip ties for mounting components to chassis
  • Small screwdriver set

How It Works

This project connects two worlds: a "thinking" AI model running on a laptop, and a "doing" robot built from Arduino. Think of it like a translator standing between a brain and a body.

First, we use a free website called Teachable Machine to train a mini AI brain. We show it pictures from a webcam (like a hand pointing left, right, or a "stop" fist) or we let it listen to spoken words ("forward", "stop"), and we tell it which class each example belongs to. After seeing enough examples, the model learns to recognise new, unseen gestures or sounds and guess which class they belong to — this is called a prediction.

The Teachable Machine model runs entirely inside the Chrome browser using JavaScript — it never touches the Arduino directly. So we add a small bridge: whenever the browser is confident about a prediction (say, "left" with high confidence), it sends a single letter like L down the USB cable using something called the Web Serial API — this lets a Chrome browser tab talk to a device plugged into a USB port, just like the Arduino Serial Monitor does.

The Arduino is running a simple sketch that constantly listens on its Serial port. When it receives a letter, it looks it up (F = forward, B = backward, L = left, R = right, S = stop) and sends the matching electrical signals to the L298N motor driver, which is powerful enough to actually spin the two DC motors — something the Arduino's own pins cannot do alone. The motors turn, and the robot moves — all because of a hand gesture or spoken word the AI recognised a second earlier.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Assemble the robot chassis: attach the two DC gear motors to the base plate, fit the wheels, and add the caster wheel at the front or back for balance.
  2. Mount the L298N motor driver and Arduino Uno onto the chassis using tape or screws, leaving the USB port accessible.
  3. Wire the motors to the L298N: left motor to OUT1/OUT2, right motor to OUT3/OUT4.
  4. Wire the L298N to the Arduino: ENA→pin 5, IN1→pin 8, IN2→pin 9, ENB→pin 6, IN3→pin 10, IN4→pin 11. Connect L298N GND to Arduino GND (common ground is essential).
  5. Connect the battery pack's positive and negative leads to the L298N's 12V and GND screw terminals. Do not power the motors from the Arduino's 5V pin — it cannot supply enough current.
  6. Upload the Arduino sketch (below) to the Uno using the USB cable. Open the Serial Monitor, set baud rate to 9600, and type F, B, L, R, S to confirm the robot responds correctly to each letter before continuing.
  7. On the laptop, open teachablemachine.withgoogle.com in Chrome and start a new Image Project (for gestures) or Audio Project (for voice commands).
  8. Create classes matching the robot's commands, e.g. Forward, Backward, Left, Right, Stop. Record at least 30-50 samples per class using the webcam or microphone, varying angle/lighting/tone slightly so the model generalises well.
  9. Click Train Model and wait for training to finish. Test each class live in the Preview panel and confirm predictions are accurate; retrain with more samples for any class the model confuses often.
  10. Export the model: choose Tensorflow.js, click Export, and either use the provided sample code or open the hosted "Export" project link. Add the Web Serial connection code (provided in the Full Code section) to the exported sketch.js so predictions above a chosen confidence threshold are converted into single-letter serial commands.
  11. Close the Arduino Serial Monitor (Chrome cannot access the COM port if it is already open elsewhere), then open the modified Teachable Machine web page in Chrome and click the "Connect to Arduino" button, selecting the correct COM port from the pop-up list.
  12. Test each gesture or spoken command in front of the webcam/microphone and observe the robot moving accordingly. Discuss with students why there is a small delay between doing the gesture and the robot responding.
  13. Fine-tune the confidence threshold and the COMMAND_TIMEOUT safety value in the Arduino sketch so the robot stops promptly when no gesture is being shown.

Full Code

// Voice/Gesture Controlled Robot - Arduino Receiver Sketch
// Waits for single-character commands sent from the Teachable Machine
// web page (via USB Serial / the Web Serial API) and drives two DC motors
// through an L298N motor driver.

// ---- Motor driver pins ----
const int ENA = 5;   // left motor speed (PWM)
const int IN1 = 8;   // left motor direction
const int IN2 = 9;
const int ENB = 6;   // right motor speed (PWM)
const int IN3 = 10;  // right motor direction
const int IN4 = 11;

const int MOTOR_SPEED = 180;   // 0-255; adjust for your motors/battery

char lastCommand = 'S';                    // most recent command letter
unsigned long lastCommandTime = 0;         // when it arrived (millis)
const unsigned long COMMAND_TIMEOUT = 600; // ms; stop if nothing new arrives

void driveLeftMotor(bool fwd, int speed) {
  digitalWrite(IN1, fwd ? HIGH : LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN2, fwd ? LOW : HIGH);
  analogWrite(ENA, speed);
}
void driveRightMotor(bool fwd, int speed) {
  digitalWrite(IN3, fwd ? HIGH : LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN4, fwd ? LOW : HIGH);
  analogWrite(ENB, speed);
}

void forward()   { driveLeftMotor(true,  MOTOR_SPEED); driveRightMotor(true,  MOTOR_SPEED); }
void backward()  { driveLeftMotor(false, MOTOR_SPEED); driveRightMotor(false, MOTOR_SPEED); }
void turnLeft()  { driveLeftMotor(false, MOTOR_SPEED); driveRightMotor(true,  MOTOR_SPEED); }
void turnRight() { driveLeftMotor(true,  MOTOR_SPEED); driveRightMotor(false, MOTOR_SPEED); }
void stopMotors(){ analogWrite(ENA, 0); analogWrite(ENB, 0); }

void applyCommand(char cmd) {
  switch (cmd) {
    case 'F': forward();    break;
    case 'B': backward();   break;
    case 'L': turnLeft();   break;
    case 'R': turnRight();  break;
    case 'S':
    default:  stopMotors(); break;
  }
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(ENA, OUTPUT); pinMode(IN1, OUTPUT); pinMode(IN2, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ENB, OUTPUT); pinMode(IN3, OUTPUT); pinMode(IN4, OUTPUT);
  stopMotors();
  Serial.begin(9600);   // must match the baud rate used by the web page
}

void loop() {
  // 1) Read any new command letter sent from the browser
  if (Serial.available() > 0) {
    char c = Serial.read();
    if (c=='F' || c=='B' || c=='L' || c=='R' || c=='S') {
      lastCommand = c;
      lastCommandTime = millis();
      applyCommand(lastCommand);
    }
  }

  // 2) Safety stop: if no fresh command has arrived recently, halt.
  // This stops a "runaway" robot if the laptop disconnects or the gesture
  // is lost, which is why we keep track of lastCommandTime.
  if (millis() - lastCommandTime > COMMAND_TIMEOUT) {
    stopMotors();
    lastCommand = 'S';
  }
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
"Connect to Arduino" in Chrome fails or sees no portThe Arduino IDE Serial Monitor is still open and holding the COM portClose the Serial Monitor, then click Connect again in Chrome
There is no "Connect" option / Web Serial does nothingUsing a browser without Web Serial support, or an insecure pageUse Google Chrome or Edge, served over https or localhost (Firefox and Safari are not supported)
Motors never moveBattery switch off, or motors powered from the Arduino 5V instead of the L298N battery inputPower the motors from the L298N 12V terminals, turn the battery on, and share GND with the Arduino
Robot moves the wrong way for a gestureA motor's wires are reversed, or a class is mapped to the wrong letterSwap that motor's OUT wires, or fix which class sends which command letter
Robot keeps driving after you stop gesturingConfidence threshold too low, or COMMAND_TIMEOUT too longRaise the confidence threshold and shorten COMMAND_TIMEOUT so it stops quickly
Predictions are unreliableToo few or too similar training samples, or poor lightingRecord 30-50 varied samples per class in the lighting and background you will actually use

Discussion Questions

  • The AI model runs in the browser, not on the Arduino. Why do we need a "bridge" that sends single letters over USB?
  • Why does the robot need a separate motor driver and battery instead of running the motors straight from the Arduino?
  • Why is the COMMAND_TIMEOUT safety stop important — what could happen without it?
  • How does showing the model more varied examples (different angles, lighting, or voices) make its predictions more reliable?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a new gesture or word (for example "spin"), map it to a new letter, and give it its own motor action.
  • Medium: Add an LED or buzzer that signals which command the robot is currently obeying.
  • Hard: Send a speed value along with the direction (for example F150) so a gesture can control how fast the robot goes, not just which way.
